questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman attended with flu-like symptoms. She had unprotected sexual intercourse with a casual partner 3 weeks before her symptoms began. Investigations: Fourth-generation HIV test positive Confirmatory anti-HIV-1 and anti-HIV-2 antibodies negative HIV viral load 3 million copies/mL
questions.lead_in: In addition to HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies, what does a fourth-generation HIV test detect?
questions.explanation: p24 antigen The fourth-generation HIV test is an ELISA testing for both HIV-1/HIV-2 antibodies as well as the p24 antigen (a capsid protein of the virus). Because the p24 antigen is detectable before HIV antibodies, fourth-generation tests can detect HIV infection earlier than tests that only detect HIV antibodies (third-generation tests).
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q33

questions.question: A 20-year-old man with lymphadenopathy; aspiration reveals Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and he does not have respiratory tuberculosis.
questions.question_raw: 20M that has lymphadenopathy. You do an aspiration and discover Mycobacterium tuberculosis. They do not have respiratory TB.

parts.text: What coinfection must you test for?
What are all the antimycobacterial medications you need to start and what are their durations?
A few weeks later he has hepatitis with transaminases 6x ULN and no other medications. What is the most likely medication to cause his hepatitis and what do you do?
At week 12 the initial lymph node is more enlarged but nontender. What is the cause?

parts_raw.text: What coinfection must you test for?
What are all the antimycobacterial medications you need to start and what are their durations? (4 points)
A few weeks later he has hepatitis, transaminases 6x ULN. He has not been taking any other medications. What is the most likely medication to cause his hepatitis and what do you do?
At week 12 he notes that the initial lymph node is more enlarged than it had been previously. It is nontender on examination but larger than it had been at diagnosis. What is the cause of this?

questions.model_answer: a) Standard precautions only; airborne isolation is not required for isolated lymph-node (extrapulmonary) TB without pulmonary/laryngeal involvement. b) HIV. c) Isoniazid (6 months), rifampin (6 months), pyrazinamide (first 2 months), ethambutol (first 2 months, until susceptibilities confirm the organism is susceptible) - i.e., 2 months RIPE then 4 months INH/RIF. d) Most likely pyrazinamide (highest hepatotoxicity of the first-line agents; INH also common). Stop all hepatotoxic drugs (INH, RIF, PZA) until aminotransferases normalize and symptoms resolve, then reintroduce stepwise with monitoring. e) A paradoxical (upgrading) reaction to therapy - not treatment failure or relapse; continue the same regimen (steroids/NSAIDs if severe).
questions.beyond_mandell: Isolation-precaution guidance for extrapulmonary TB is from CDC/PHAC infection control, not the chapter.

needs: Chapter 131 — Management of Opportunistic Infections in HIV
questions.question: A patient with HIV has a CD4 count of 62 cells/mm3 and a viral load of 250,000 copies/mL, serology showing immunity to hepatitis B, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.
questions.question_raw: HIV patient with CD4 62, viral load 250K. Immune HBV serology. Infection with PJP.

parts.text: When should antiretroviral therapy be started, and why?
Give six screening tests indicated as part of her initial HIV assessment.

parts_raw.text: When to start ARVs? And why?
Give 6 screening tests indicated as part of her initial HIV assessment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Start ART within the first 2 weeks of beginning PCP treatment. Longer delay is associated with additional opportunistic infections and decreased survival; the exact day within that window depends on severity, ability to absorb oral drugs, and drug interactions. (PCP is not one of the exceptions - cryptococcal or tuberculous meningitis is deferred 2-10 weeks; cryptosporidiosis and JC virus encephalitis are started as soon as feasible.) Caution: ART may worsen pulmonary function through IRIS as the recovering inflammatory response meets residual Pneumocystis antigen.
b) (1) Screening test for latent tuberculosis (TST or IGRA). (2) Toxoplasma gondii IgG serology (determines need for toxoplasmosis prophylaxis at CD4 <100). (3) Hepatitis B serology - anti-HBs/anti-HBc to define immunity and vaccination need (already immune here). (4) Hepatitis A serology to identify HAV-susceptible patients needing vaccination. (5) Coccidioides IgM/IgG serology if she lives in an endemic area (prophylaxis if positive and CD4 <250). (6) VZV serology/history of varicella or zoster to determine vaccine or post-exposure candidacy. Also: syphilis serology, and CD4 count/viral load monitoring to guide starting and stopping prophylaxis.
questions.beyond_mandell: Serum cryptococcal antigen screening at CD4 <100 and G6PD testing before dapsone are standard DHHS/IDSA OI-guideline additions not specified in this chapter text.

cohort_answer.text:
When to start ARVs: ASAP, within 2 weeks of dx of PCP – associated with lower death. In an RCT of 282 patients with OIs other than TB, 63% of whom had definite or presumptive PCP, a significantly lower incidence of AIDS progression or death (a secondary study endpoint) was seen in subjects randomized to early (median 12 days after initiation of therapy for OI) versus deferred initiation of ART (median 45 days). Of note, no patients with PCP and respiratory failure requiring intubation were enrolled in the study, and initiating ART in such patients is problematic due to the lack of parenteral preparations and unpredictble absorption of oral medications, as well as potential drug interactions with agents commonly used in the ICU
Six screening tests: Hep C serology; Baseline labs: CBC, LFTs, renal function; Cryptococcal antigen serum; TST / IGRA; Syphilis Screening; Gonorrhea and Chlamydia screen; HPV; VZV if no clear history of chicken pox +/- immunization; Toxo; G6PD screen (in case can't use TMP-SMX); Hep A (more in MSM)

questions.question: A point-of-care HIV test has a sensitivity and specificity of 99%.
questions.question_raw: POC HIV test with sens and spec of 99 percent.

parts.text: Calculate the negative predictive value and positive predictive value in a population with a point prevalence of 1%.
Provide an argument in favour of and one against using this test.

parts_raw.text: Calculate the the NPV and PPV in a population with point prevalence of 1%.
Provide an argument in favor and one against using this test.

questions.model_answer:
a) Take 10,000 people at 1% prevalence: 100 infected, 9900 uninfected.
True positives = 0.99 x 100 = 99; false negatives = 1.
True negatives = 0.99 x 9900 = 9801; false positives = 99.
PPV = TP/(TP+FP) = 99/(99+99) = 99/198 = 50%.
NPV = TN/(TN+FN) = 9801/(9801+1) = 9801/9802 = 99.99% (~100%).
So only half of positives are true positives, while a negative essentially excludes infection.

b) In favour: it is a rapid/simple single-visit assay (result in <15-30 min) usable at the point of care with fingerstick or oral fluid and little equipment, which markedly increases the proportion of people who actually receive their result (pregnant women in labour, STI and outpatient clinics, emergency departments) and permits immediate counselling and linkage; with NPV ~100% at this prevalence a nonreactive result reliably rules out established infection.
Against: at 1% prevalence the PPV is only 50%, so half of reactive results are false positives, causing profound patient distress and further testing - no single test is adequate in a low-prevalence population; a reactive result must be followed by a highly specific supplemental assay. Rapid tests are also less sensitive than conventional assays in seroconversion panels (positive 2-8 days later; the fourth-generation rapid assay detects p24 in only ~10%), so acute HIV would be missed.

cohort_answer.text: As prevalence of disease is low NPV is better. For any given test (i.e. sensitivity and specificity remain the same) as prevalence decreases, the PPV decreases because there will be more false positives for every true positive.
